Title: Clinical implications of understanding the association between oxidative stress and pediatric NAFLD.

Abstract: Oxidative stress is central to the pathogenesis of non-alcoholic steatohepatitis. The reactive oxygen species (ROS) that characterise oxidative stress are generated in several cellular sites and their production is influence by multi-organ interactions. Areas covered: Mitochondrial dysfunction is the main source of ROS in fatty liver and is closely related to endoplasmic reticulum stress. Both are caused by lipotoxicity and together these three factors form a cycle of progressive organelle damage, resulting in sterile inflammation and apoptosis. Adipose tissue inflammation and intestinal dysbiosis provide substrates for ROS formation and trigger immune activation. Obstructive sleep apnea and abnormal divalent metal metabolism may also play a role. Expert commentary: The majority of available high-quality data originates from studies in adults and there are fewer therapeutic trials performed in pediatric cohorts, therefore conclusions are generalised to children. === PMID: 27501738 ===

Title: Nocturnal hypoxia-induced oxidative stress promotes progression of pediatric non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.

Journal/Date: Journal of hepatology (2016)

MeSH Keywords: Adolescent, Aldehydes, Child, F2-Isoprostanes, Humans, Hypoxia, Liver, Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease


--- ABSTRACT ---
[BACKGROUND & AIMS]: Oxidative stress is proposed as a central mediator in NAFLD pathogenesis, but the specific trigger for reactive oxygen species generation has not been clearly delineated. In addition, emerging evidence shows that obesity related obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) and nocturnal hypoxia are associated with NAFLD progression in adults. The aim of this study was to determine if OSA/nocturnal hypoxia-induced oxidative stress promotes the progression of pediatric NAFLD.
[METHODS]: Subjects with biopsy proven NAFLD and lean controls were studied. Subjects underwent polysomnograms, liver histology scoring, laboratory testing, urine F(2)-isoprostanes (measure of lipid peroxidation) and 4-hydroxynonenal liver immunohistochemistry (in situ hepatic lipid peroxidation).
[RESULTS]: We studied 36 adolescents with NAFLD and 14 lean controls. The OSA/hypoxia group (69% of NAFLD subjects) had more severe fibrosis (64% stage 0-2; 36% stage 3) than those without OSA/hypoxia (100% stage 0-2), p=0.03. Higher F(2)-isoprostanes correlated with apnea/hypoxia index (r=0.39, p=0.03), % time SaO2 <90% (r=0.56, p=0.0008) and inversely with SaO2 nadir (r=-0.46, p=0.008). OSA/hypoxia was most severe in subjects with the greatest 4HNE staining (p=0.03). Increasing F(2)-isoprostanes(r=0.32, p=0.04) and 4HNE hepatic staining (r=0.47, p=0.007) were associated with worsening steatosis. Greater oxidative stress occurred in subjects with definite NASH as measured by F(2)-isoprostanes (p=0.06) and hepatic 4HNE (p=0.03) compared to those with borderline/not NASH.
[CONCLUSIONS]: These data support the role of nocturnal hypoxia as a trigger for localized hepatic oxidative stress, an important factor associated with the progression of NASH and hepatic fibrosis in obese pediatric patients.
[LAY SUMMARY]: Obstructive sleep apnea and low nighttime oxygen are associated with NAFLD progression in adults. In this study, we show that adolescents with NAFLD who have OSA and low oxygen have significant scar tissue in their livers. NAFLD subjects affected by OSA and low oxygen have a greater imbalance between the production of free radicals and their body's ability to counteract their harmful effects than subjects without OSA and low oxygen. This study shows that low oxygen levels may be an important trigger in the progression of pediatric NASH.

Title: Association between obstructive sleep apnea and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease in pediatric patients: a meta-analysis.

Journal/Date: Pediatric obesity (2021)

MeSH Keywords: Adolescent, Child, Cross-Sectional Studies, Humans, Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease, Sleep Apnea, Obstructive


--- ABSTRACT ---
[BACKGROUND]: Some studies have reported a relationship between obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) in pediatric population. However, this issue remains controversial.
[OBJECTIVES]: The purpose of the present study was to investigate the association between OSA and NAFLD in pediatric population.
[METHODS]: We systematically searched PubMed, Web of Science, Embase for eligible studies. The data involving markers of NAFLD including alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), hepatic inflammation, hepatic fibrosis of both OSA group and control group were extracted. Pooled standardised mean difference (SMD) and weighted mean difference (WMD) were appropriately calculated through a fixed or random-effect model.
[RESULTS]: Nine cross-sectional studies with 1133 children and adolescents were included. OSA was significantly associated with ALT, AST, and NAFLD fibrosis stage, but not NAFLD inflammation grade. Subgroup analysis indicated that both mild OSA and severe OSA were significantly associated with elevated ALT and AST. Furthermore, in the studies with all main confounding factors (age, gender, and BMI) matched, OSA group had higher ALT and AST levels than control group.
[CONCLUSIONS]: This meta-analysis suggested that OSA was associated with NAFLD evidenced by elevated liver enzymes and progressive hepatic fibrosis in pediatric population. Screening and monitoring of NAFLD in pediatric patients with obesity-related OSA are necessary.

key_findings.finding: The strongest pediatric human evidence supports an association between nocturnal hypoxia/OSA and more advanced NAFLD. In a biopsy-based adolescent study (PMID 27501738; n=36 NAFLD, 14 lean controls), 69% had OSA/hypoxia; affected participants had more stage-3 fibrosis than those without OSA/hypoxia (36% vs 0%, p=0.03). Higher urinary F2-isoprostanes correlated with apnea/hypoxia index, time with SaO2 <90%, and lower oxygen nadir; hepatic 4-hydroxynonenal staining correlated with hypoxia severity and steatosis. Oxidative stress was greater in definite NASH. This directly supports nocturnal hypoxemia as a plausible oxidative-stress-linked promoter of pediatric NASH/fibrosis, but the study is observational and small.

Pediatric aggregate evidence is directionally positive but largely cross-sectional. A meta-analysis of 9 cross-sectional studies including 1,133 children/adolescents (PMID 32881371) found OSA associated with higher ALT, AST, and NAFLD fibrosis stage, but not histologic inflammation grade; associations with ALT/AST persisted in studies matched for age, sex, and BMI. This strengthens the association beyond obesity alone, but does not establish progression or causality.

A pediatric obesity cohort (PMID 34828697; n=153, mean age 10.5 years, all with OSA) found hepatic steatosis in 69 children, with mild-to-severe grades. AHI correlated with ALT independent of age, sex, BMI-SDS, waist, and HOMA-IR (r²=0.10, p=0.0003), but the association disappeared after adjustment for hepatic steatosis; the relationship was confined to children with steatosis and strengthened with steatosis severity. Thus OSA appears linked primarily to liver injury in children who already have steatosis, while residual confounding and reverse directionality remain possible.

key_findings.finding: The pediatric intervention signal is consistent with causality but is very preliminary. In 9 biopsy-proven pediatric NAFLD patients with OSA/hypoxia (PMID 29752170), approximately 89 days of CPAP improved sleep-disordered breathing despite BMI increasing and was accompanied by lower ALT, metabolic-syndrome markers, and urinary F2-isoprostanes. The uncontrolled, very small before-after design cannot separate CPAP effects from regression to the mean or other changes, and histologic reversal was not demonstrated.

source_tools.relevance: pediatric CPAP treatment, ALT and oxidative-stress biomarker response

key_findings.finding: A complementary pediatric biopsy study (PMID 31334441; n=31 adolescents with NAFLD, 68% with OSA and/or hypoxia) found nocturnal hypoxia associated with hepatic Sonic hedgehog/Gli2 and α-SMA activation, K7, and HIF-1α-related signaling; these markers correlated with AST/ALT, NAFLD activity, and hypoxia/desaturation measures. This supports a hypoxia-to-HIF/hedgehog/epithelial-mesenchymal-transition/fibrogenic mechanism, although it is not a direct oxidative-stress assay and the cohort was predominantly obese (mean BMI z-score 2.2), so obesity/metabolic disease remain important co-drivers.

source_tools.relevance: pediatric liver biopsy mechanistic study linking hypoxia to fibrogenic signaling and enzymes

key_findings.finding: Additional pediatric biomarker evidence shows biologic plausibility but is less liver-specific: in 58 obese children (PMID 26298775), sCD163, a macrophage-activation marker relevant to NAFLD, increased stepwise with OSA severity and correlated strongly with AHI (rho 0.71, p<0.001); it decreased after tonsillectomy in six severe-OSA patients. The study did not directly stage steatosis/fibrosis or measure oxidative stress, so it supports inflammatory pressure rather than proving liver progression.

source_tools.relevance: pediatric OSA severity and macrophage-activation biomarker

key_findings.finding: Obesity is a major confounder and shared substrate: the key pediatric cohorts were predominantly obese, and OSA, insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, and NAFLD cluster together. However, the biopsy oxidative-stress study linked F2-isoprostanes and 4-HNE specifically to hypoxemia metrics, and the meta-analysis found higher ALT/AST even in age/sex/BMI-matched comparisons. The most defensible conclusion is that OSA/nocturnal intermittent hypoxia likely adds an independent aggravating signal—especially for oxidative stress and fibrosis—on top of obesity-related NAFLD, but pediatric evidence remains small, observational, and insufficient to prove that OSA alone initiates MASLD.

Adult evidence is broader and more mechanistically developed, but should not be substituted for pediatric evidence. The adult-focused review (PMID 27324067) summarizes chronic intermittent hypoxia effects on insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, HIF-1α/lipogenesis, β-oxidation and hepatic oxidative stress, while noting no definitive proof that CPAP improves NAFLD. Pediatric studies provide direct human links to fibrosis, ALT/AST, F2-isoprostanes/4-HNE, and hypoxia-related fibrogenic signaling, but lack large longitudinal cohorts and randomized CPAP trials.
